definition: Cheerful and friendly in a warm, hearty, good-humored way.
example: The jovial baker chatted with every customer while boxing up their pastries.
nuance: Jovial suggests hearty, outgoing good cheer among company; genial is warm and kind but quieter, and jocular means given to joking.
prompt: A grandfather welcomes relatives arriving for a big holiday dinner.
options: Grandpa greeted every guest with a jovial laugh and a firm handshake.
Grandpa gave a jovial frown and told the children to stop talking.
Grandpa stayed jovial by refusing to speak to anyone at the table.
Grandpa wrote a jovial schedule listing the exact minute each dish would come out.
reasons: A hearty laugh and warm welcome show exactly this kind of sociable good cheer.
A frown and a scolding are stern, which contradicts a cheerful, friendly mood.
The word describes outgoing friendliness, so silent withdrawal reverses its meaning.
A precise timetable has no mood; the word describes cheerful people or their manner.

practice.prompt: A tour guide leads a group of visitors through a city on a rainy afternoon.
options: The guide was so jovial that she burst into tears when the rain began.
The jovial map showed every street in tiny gray print.
Despite the drizzle, the jovial guide kept everyone laughing with tales about the old bridge.
The jovial guide muttered complaints and walked ahead without looking back.
reasons: Crying from disappointment signals sadness, not good humor.
A map cannot feel cheerful; the word fits people and their behavior, not objects like this.
Keeping spirits high with humor in bad weather shows hearty, friendly cheer.
Grumbling and ignoring the group is gloomy and unfriendly, the opposite of the word.
